items.title: Port of Savannah Wins Approval for $2.3 Billion Container Terminal
items.original_title: Port of Savannah Wins Approval for $2.3 Billion Container Terminal
items.summary: The Georgia Ports Authority has secured federal approval for a new $2.3 billion container terminal in Savannah, clearing a major hurdle in its plan to expand the port’s annual handling capacity to 12 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs). Army Corps of Engineers approved the Savannah Container Terminal permit following a three-year review, Georgia Ports President Kevin Price announced Wednesday at the authority’s annual State of the Port of Savannah event. The project is a centerpiece of Georgia Ports’ nearly $5 billion infrastructure investment plan for the next decade, which includes five additional large containership berths in Savannah and expanded roll-on/roll-off capacity at the Port of Brunswick. Another major piece of that expansion is already underway at Savannah’s Ocean Terminal, where a $1.6 billion redevelopment will increase annual container capacity from 200,000 TEUs to 1.75 million TEUs. “Our $5 billion investment in future port infrastructure is the largest in the nation and a reassuring roadmap to customers which comes on the heels of our $4.13 billion investment the last ten years in port and inland infrastructure,” Georgia Ports Authority Chairman Alec Poitevint said. The port handled a record 504,015 TEUs in September , up 3.7% from a year earlier, pushing container traffic for the first quarter of its fiscal year above 1.5 million TEUs.

items.title: Slash emissions with shipping: New report shows coastal shipping can help reduce freight emissions and bolster Australia’s supply chain resilience
items.original_title: Slash emissions with shipping: New report shows coastal shipping can help reduce freight emissions and bolster Australia’s supply chain resilience
items.summary: Up to 90 per cent of freight emissions can be cut simply by moving more cargo to coastal shipping, a new independent report reveals. Comparing the emissions performance of road, rail and shipping across four essential Australian freight routes, The Emission Reduction Potential of Mode Shift to Maritime Transport report found greenhouse gas emissions reductions of between 60 to 90 per cent by rebalancing freight between road and coastal shipping. Launched at Parliament House today by the Hon. Catherine King, the report was developed by Transport Emissions/Energy Research and commissioned by the Maritime Union of Australia in collaboration with Maritime Industry Australia Limited (MIAL) and supported by the Energy Futures Foundation. Clare Grandison, Principal Advisor – Decarbonisation and Industry Transformation, said the report shows significant diesel fuel use and emissions reductions are possible using today’s technology and maritime footprint. “The Australian transport sector is a significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, making up more than 21 per cent of total emissions each year. The report shows emissions reductions are feasible now, using today’s vessels, infrastructure and capability.” Angela Gillham, CEO of MIAL, said the said greater use of coastal shipping could improve productivity for the freight sector and strengthen supply chain resilience.

items.summary: Shipping containers are seen at the port of Barcelona, Spain, October 3, 2024. REUTERS/Nacho Doce The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) is proposing $200,000 fees on Spanish-flagged vessels entering American ports, along with restrictions on billions of dollars in Spanish imports, after concluding that Spain’s refusal to admit certain U.S.-flagged ships has created unfavorable conditions for American shipping. The proposed measures include a $200,000 fee each time a Spanish-flagged vessel enters a U.S. port from abroad, as well as potential restrictions on imports of Spanish cosmetics, oils and fats, ceramics, stone products, and sugar and confectionery. The dispute began in November 2024, when Spanish authorities refused port access to the U.S.-flagged Maersk Denver and Maersk Seletar , both operated by Maersk Line, Limited, over cargo connected to Israel. The regulator said the restrictions undermine the ability of U.S.-flagged ships to compete for cargo moving to and from Spain, while also affecting vessels that could be called upon to support U.S. The Commission has now narrowed its proposed vessel fee to $200,000 per voyage while identifying specific categories of Spanish goods that could face import restrictions. The FMC said the proposed penalties are intended to address shipping conditions created by Spain’s port restrictions, rather than the broader political dispute over the transportation of military cargo to Israel.

items.summary: Aristides Pittas-led EuroDry has returned to China’s Hengli Shipbuilding for another kamsarmax, adding a third 82,000 dwt newbuilding to a fleet renewal programme now worth almost $183m. The Nasdaq-listed dry bulk owner is paying about $37m for the latest vessel, which is scheduled for delivery in the third quarter of 2029. The ship will be built to an eco design compliant with EEDI Phase 3 requirements and will follow two sister vessels already booked at Hengli for delivery in the first and second quarters of 2028. Those earlier ships were contracted in April and May this year for a combined $74m, also working out at $37m apiece. In addition to the three Hengli kamsarmaxes, the company has two 63,500 dwt ultramaxes under construction at Nantong Xiangyu Shipbuilding. The Aristeidis and Troboni are due in the second and third quarters of 2027 and cost $71.8m in total. EuroDry currently operates 11 bulkers totalling 766,420 dwt, including two kamsarmaxes, six supra/ultramaxes and three older panamaxes. On the current fleet count, delivery of all five ships would take EuroDry to 16 bulkers with around 1.14m dwt of capacity. Hengli has attracted a growing list of Greek dry bulk owners in recent years, with Star Bulk, Oceanbulk, Laskaridis Maritime and others turning to the revived Dalian yard for kamsarmax tonnage.

items.original_title: GFS ship sinks after missile attack, second ship sustains damage
items.summary: Missiles struck two container ships in Global Feeder Shipping’s (GFS) fleet in the Strait of Hormuz in the last 24 hours, with one vessel subsequently sinking after catching fire. Singapore’s Maritime and Port Authority (MPA) said that the 2008-built 2,824 teu GFS Pride was damaged and caught fire before sinking. All of its 21 crewmen were evacuated, with no injuries reported. The other ship, 2015-built 4,350 teu GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage but remained operational and proceeded under its own power to a safe anchorage. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said an unnamed container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers had struck a mine while transiting what it described as an “unauthorised and dangerous” route through the strait. The sinking of GFS Pride is the second vessel loss since the US-Israel-Iran war began on 28 February, according to data from the International Maritime Organization, the United Nations’ shipping agency. The earlier incident involved a bulk carrier, Cape Dao, which sank in the Gulf of Oman yesterday, after being hit by two torpedoes on 23 September. Both GFS Pride and GFS Giselle were originally owned by Dubai-based Simatech Shipping, before the latter’s liner operations were acquired by GFS in October 2018.

items.title: Cyber-crime group hits 38 shipping and port groups with data leak threat
items.original_title: Cyber-crime group hits 38 shipping and port groups with data leak threat
items.summary: Cyber extortion group ‘n0n’ has named 38 organisations across the global shipping and ports sector on its dark-web leak site, raising concerns that data may have been stolen. Cybersecurity firm SOCRadar reported yesterday n0n published the listings in a single batch on 12 October, that included container terminals, shipping lines, port IT providers, and logistics businesses across 18 countries. The group emerged last month, listing 21 organisations across sectors including telecoms, retail, pharmaceuticals, and education. SOCRadar said the pattern of data described in the listings suggested a possible common point of entry, rather than 38 separate network intrusions. The amounts did not appear to correspond with the volume of data allegedly stolen: EUSU Logistics faced a $14m demand for 60mb, with ILCS Pelindo at $2.4m for 2.4gb. Of its 21 earlier victims, SOCRadar said 19 remained at the claimed stage, one was listed as negotiating, and one, Chibitek, had experienced a data leak. SOCRadar warned that maritime businesses that exchange EDI with companies named in the attack should plan for the possibility that their operational data could appear in the 19 October release. It advised them to identify the port community systems, EDI hubs, and file-transfer services handling their data; to check with providers for potential breaches, patch exposed systems, and investigate unusual access or bulk downloads.

items.summary: A ship’s anchor can wreak havoc on the world’s undersea infrastructure, something that has provided plenty of rich material for Splash reporting in recent years. On Christmas Day 2024, the vessel was accused of dragging its anchor 90 km across the Gulf of Finland seabed, severing the Estlink 2 power link and four telecommunications cables before Finnish authorities intervened. That collision between maritime law and an emerging security threat runs through Braw’s new book, The Undersea War: The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World , published by John Murray this month. Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads research into threats to the global maritime order, started writing in October 2024, having followed the subject for considerably longer. The 2022 Nord Stream pipeline explosions remain in the headlines. The Eagle S affair followed the Yi Peng 3 cable investigation and has been succeeded by further suspected anchor-dragging incidents in the Baltic. The book ranges from the Baltic to the Pacific, drawing on interviews with naval officers, undersea engineers and cable operators to show just how dependent modern economies have become on infrastructure that is difficult to monitor and harder still to defend.

items.title: The Confidence To Act: Why R&D And Lifecycle Support Are The Real Enablers Of Fleet Decarbonisation
items.original_title: The Confidence To Act: Why R&D And Lifecycle Support Are The Real Enablers Of Fleet Decarbonisation
items.summary: Industry analysis suggests that roughly two-thirds of the existing global fleet will not undergo major retrofits for next-generation fuels, primarily because of vessel age and the economics involved. For this majority, the industry needs solutions that deliver measurable emissions reductions today, without introducing operational risk or requiring capital commitments that cannot be justified. One approach to this challenge is in adopting a layered strategy, one that matches the right solution to the right vessel, at the right point in its lifecycle. Fuel supply systems are an enabler of that strategy, and the confidence to invest in them depends, more than anything else, on the quality of the engineering, R&D and lifecycle support that underpins them. Documented, applied research into how alternative fuels behave in practice, and how fuel supply systems must be designed to handle them, is the foundation on which ship owner confidence is built. This is why lifecycle services are integral to the value of any decarbonisation investment, not an optional extra. In a sector defined by long asset cycles and the need to make durable capital decisions under uncertainty, that matters. R&D provides the foundation, and lifecycle support sustains it. Together, they give ship owners the confidence that their decarbonisation strategy remains resilient as the transition unfolds.

items.title: Look beyond AI productivity gains, forwarders told
items.original_title: Look beyond AI productivity gains, forwarders told
items.summary: Freight forwarders should focus on using artificial intelligence to capture lost gross profit and deliver more tailored customer service, rather than treating the technology primarily as a productivity tool, according to Erik Muttersbach, founder of AI software company Zauber. Speaking on The Loadstar Podcast , Mr Muttersbach said AI could transform freight forwarding into a higher-value, higher-margin business over the next three to five years, with a growing divide between companies that adopt the technology quickly and those that struggle to keep pace. Mr Muttersbach said 2025 saw a wave of AI start-ups and funding announcements, while 2026 has been characterised by companies running pilots and proofs of concept, alongside industry leaders committing to larger-scale deployments. He highlighted that rather than using AI to increase productivity, forwarders should instead target opportunities to improve profitability. AI could also help forwarders deliver on complex customer-specific requirements that have traditionally been difficult to manage consistently across global operations. “There’s an opportunity to do incredibly individual customer service every single time,” he stressed, and underscored that forwarders that continue offering only standardised services risk losing their competitive edge as customers increasingly expect individualised service to become the norm.

items.summary: Transpacific container freight rates are likely to remain higher than on Asia-Europe for some time, as stronger economic conditions in the US support import demand and weaker European growth weighs on cargo volumes and freight rates. Evergreen general manager Wu Kuang Hui said the rate divergence had become increasingly pronounced: “strong on US routes, weak on Europe routes”. And he said on Friday he expected the stronger US market to continue supporting transpacific rates at a premium to Asia-Europe rates, and there was “no reason to be pessimistic” about the US routes before the lunar new year 2027 as “there are record-high import volumes at several major US ports, low inventory levels, and optimistic consumer demand”. US imports from the Far East have grown about 5.1%, but volumes to Europe have increased more rapidly, by 12.2%. On Friday, the Shanghai Containerised Freight Index showed Shanghai-US east and west coast rates relatively stable, at $10,524 and $7,584 per 40ft, respectively. Shanghai-Europe rates continued to decline, losing 3%, to $2,274 per teu. By contrast, transpacific capacity remains supported by robust US import demand. Mr Wu noted that US spot rates were significantly higher than negotiated rates in Q4 last year, and expects long-term contract prices next year to exceed this year’s.

items.summary: A changing fuel landscape The fuels powering vessels have shifted sharply in recent years, and the first shift was regulatory. Heavy fuel oil made up about 79% of international shipping fuel consumption in 20181 until the International Maritime Organization (IMO) cut the sulfur limit from 3.50% to 0.50% in 2020.2 Singapore, the world’s largest bunkering port and an indicator of the global market, shows how fast the market moved: low-sulfur fuel oil rose from under 1% of bunker sales in 2018 to 63% in 2020.3 Then the market shifted again. Scrubbers brought high-sulfur fuel back,3 and HSFO reached 29.5% of fuels tested by Veritas Petroleum Services (VPS) in 2023,4 alongside 54.3% VLSFO and 14.2% MGO. Biofuel blends, LNG, LPG, and methanol add further fuel types, and biofuel volumes tested by VPS rose 50% in 2025, to 1.2 million MT.5 Regulation, which triggered the previous shifts, is now driving the next one. Expanded fuel types in IMOS To keep pace with these shifts, IMOS now supports up to ten fuel types per vessel, up from six. The same limit applies to time charter contracts, so a long-term charter can reflect the vessel’s full fuel configuration.

items.title: 1 in 12 Ocean Shipments Has a Blank Carrier ETA
items.original_title: 1 in 12 Ocean Shipments Has a Blank Carrier ETA
items.summary: Tradlinx, a supply chain data platform based in South Korea, today released findings from an analysis of more than 500,000 ocean container shipments a year, showing that carrier ETAs are not only inaccurate but frequently missing. Carriers left the ETA blank in 42,832 cases, or 8.43% of shipments, most often while cargo was waiting at a transshipment port. Across more than 500,000 shipments a year, carriers left the ETA blank in 42,832 cases. The ETA for the intermediate transshipment port was missing in 30,929 cases (6.09%), the final-destination ETA of transshipment cargo in 6,168 cases (1.21%), and the destination ETA of direct shipments in 5,735 cases (1.13%). In this group of 25,341 shipments (4.99%), the average carrier ETA error was 90.0 hours. Our data points to a more basic gap: for roughly one in twelve shipments, the ETA simply goes missing somewhere along the way,” Tradlinx said. The model produced an estimate wherever the carrier ETA was missing, and its average error came in 31.4% lower than that of carrier ETAs, at 10.6 hours versus 15.4 hours. The difference was largest where carrier ETAs went furthest off course: on shipments missed by 48 hours or more, average error fell from 90.0 hours to 9.2 hours.

Looking ahead, what will AI actually change across the forwarding value chain – and which parts of the industry will prove hardest to transform? items.title: Iran threatens ships going dark in Hormuz
items.original_title: Iran threatens ships going dark in Hormuz
items.summary: Iran has warned that merchant ships switching off their identification and tracking equipment during what it deems unauthorised passages through the Strait of Hormuz will be treated as hostile, raising the stakes for vessels navigating one of the world’s most dangerous stretches of water. The warning comes as fresh details emerge of a wave of attacks on Sunday that extended beyond tankers to containerships. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) issued four retrospective alerts on Monday covering three tankers and a containership struck on October 11, bringing the day’s reported total to six. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), meanwhile, claimed to have attacked a VLCC attempting to transit without permission, releasing footage purportedly showing the fire-damaged, 298,800 dwt Al Maqam , owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services. It remains unclear whether the purported strike was among those reported by UKMTO or represents another incident. Two Indian seafarers remain missing after Sunday’s drone strike on the Nicaragua-flagged Petro Dolphin off Sohar, Oman. Nine crewmembers were rescued. The latest violence follows Saturday’s American airstrike against the Panama-flagged Ocean Molica in the Gulf of Oman, with Washington accusing the vessel of attempting to breach its naval blockade of Iranian ports.

items.summary: Petros Panagiotidis-controlled Robin Energy has taken a minority stake in Trafigura-backed Volare Shipping, adding indirect exposure to the VLCC market through the newly listed Oslo tanker owner. The Nasdaq-listed LPG carrier owner disclosed in a US Securities and Exchange Commission filing that it had participated in Volare’s private placement. Robin acquired 90,000 shares at NOK154 each, putting the investment at NOK13.86m ($1.45m). The investment follows Volare’s $500m capital raise and its move onto Euronext Growth Oslo earlier this month. Trafigura launched the shipping company in September to hold its expanding VLCC portfolio. Volare raised approximately $500m through an oversubscribed equity placement priced at NOK154 per share, valuing the company at around NOK11.5bn ($1.2bn) after the fundraising. The proceeds are intended to support outstanding newbuilding commitments, debt reduction and other corporate requirements. The company previously held a tanker alongside its gas carriers before selling that vessel earlier this year. In September, affiliated owner Toro outlined another fleet reshuffle involving the proposed separation of its remaining LPG vessels into a standalone Nasdaq-listed company.

items.title: French marines swoop on former Sovcomflot tanker in the Indian Ocean
items.original_title: French marines swoop on former Sovcomflot tanker in the Indian Ocean
items.summary: France has taken its crackdown on Russia’s shadow fleet into the Indian Ocean, boarding a former Sovcomflot aframax more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion. French marines descended by helicopter onto the 110,119 dwt DF Peak on Monday after authorities questioned the validity of its claimed Benin registration. President Emmanuel Macron said the vessel was suspected of sailing under a false flag and involvement in illicit fuel transportation. “France is determined to combat the shadow fleet, wherever it may be in the world,” Macron declared. The French military said the boarding was conducted under Article 110 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which permits inspections of vessels suspected of lacking valid nationality. Built in 2006, the tanker previously traded as NS Captain for Russian state-controlled Sovcomflot before becoming Kaliningrad in 2024 and subsequently DF Peak. The vessel has been under EU sanctions since June 2024 and is also blacklisted by Washington and London. Ukrainian intelligence links the ship to Russian crude exports. The operation follows several French interventions against Russia-linked tankers in European waters, including the interception of the Deliver off Sicily in June.

items.title: Washington teams up with ABS to accelerate nuclear shipping
items.original_title: Washington teams up with ABS to accelerate nuclear shipping
items.summary: The US Department of Energy (DOE) has joined forces with classification society ABS to accelerate the development of commercial nuclear-powered shipping and floating power plants. The agreement with DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy covers feasibility studies for floating reactors, dedicated nuclear shipping corridors and the ports, shipyards and industrial infrastructure required to build and support nuclear-powered vessels. ABS will co-manage the Maritime Nuclear Applications Group, providing technical, regulatory and economic expertise, while coordinating related work through the US Maritime Administration’s Center for Maritime Innovation. “Advanced nuclear technology is moving from concept to application, and the maritime industry needs to be ready for it,” said ABS chairman and CEO John McDonald. In 2022, DOE contracted ABS to examine barriers to commercial nuclear propulsion, while the class society subsequently published the industry’s first comprehensive rules for floating nuclear power plants. As Splash reported in July, ABS approved in principle a South Korean 15,000 teu containership concept incorporating a molten salt reactor, following earlier approvals for floating nuclear power modules developed by HD Hyundai. Last month, ABS backed a study examining the economics of a 174,000 cu m nuclear-powered LNG carrier. The vessel would cost approximately 2.5 times as much to build as a conventional LNG carrier, although researchers projected lower lifetime costs under certain carbon-pricing scenarios.

items.title: Soaring Tanker Rates Leave Americas Awash in Crude Oil
items.original_title: Soaring Tanker Rates Leave Americas Awash in Crude Oil
items.summary: HOUSTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) – Dense heavy crude, which oil refiners around the world favor for its typically low cost, is piling up in the Americas as soaring freight rates have stifled exports and US refiners have been running close to their limits. The glut in North and South America has opened an unusual split in the global oil market, as buyers in Asia and Europe struggle with supply shortages and benchmark prices hold above $100 a barrel. Heavy crude is a denser type of oil that Asian, many US, and some European refineries are typically configured to process. Flagship Canadian, Colombian and Ecuadorian heavy crude grades have all eased more than $10a barrel to trade at their lowest level in six weeks, according to price reporting agency Argus Media. The cost of a tanker from the Americas to Asia rose to more than $80 million, or about $40 a barrel, last week compared with around $10-15 million near the start of the year. Cokers convert residual crude oil into feedstocks for diesel and gasoline production, and a heavier crude slate requires them to run at a higher capacity. Many US refineries are also configured for offshore Gulf of Mexico crude such as Mars Sour, rather than Canadian or Venezuelan oil that must be mixed with lighter feedstock.

REUTERS/Stringer The European Union has imposed sanctions on some of Russia’s most important shipyards, including major submarine builders, naval ship-repair facilities and yards involved in commercial vessel construction, as part of a sweeping expansion of restrictions targeting the country’s military-industrial complex. The new sanctions , adopted Monday, add 826 Russian companies and 743 executives to the EU’s sanctions list. The measures represent the largest single expansion of the bloc’s sanctions listings since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The shipbuilding measures form one part of a much larger sanctions expansion focused heavily on Russia’s weapons production capacity. items.title: Shippers warned: spot rates no pointer to wider box shipping market
items.original_title: Shippers warned: spot rates no pointer to wider box shipping market
items.summary: Spot rates have become more volatile, relative to the wider box shipping market, since the pandemic, with overall prices increasingly diverging from signals provided by the spot market. In its latest analysis, Sea-Intelligence, compared spot rate movements on the Asia-Europe and transpacific trades with broader market developments, using World Container Index (WCI) and Container Trade Statistics (CTS) data. The consultant compared monthly average WCI rates for Shanghai-Rotterdam and Shanghai-Genoa with CTS data for Asia-Europe. Sea-Intelligence used this relationship to forecast the overall market rate index from spot rate movements, and then compared its predictions with the actual CTS figures. Before the pandemic disruptions, Sea-Intelligence found, the difference between forecast and actual market rates fluctuated relatively little, suggesting spot rates provided a reasonably reliable indication of wider market developments. However, deviations became substantially larger from 2020, which the analyst said reflected a greater disconnect between spot rate movements and the market as a whole – also evident when fluctuations were measured relative to overall rate levels, meaning it could not simply be attributed to higher freight rates. Sea-Intelligence also identified a gradual upward trend in the difference between forecast and actual rates on Asia-Europe, indicating that the overall market increasingly recorded higher rates than would have been predicted from spot prices alone.

items.summary: European natural gas prices have remained relatively contained despite major disruptions to Middle Eastern liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports, as additional supply and weaker demand have cushioned the impact, according to UBS analysts. In an October 5 report, UBS said higher LNG production outside the Middle East and reduced consumption across Europe and Asia had helped offset supply losses caused by the Iran war. Middle Eastern LNG supply declined by approximately 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) between March and September, while additional production elsewhere contributed nearly 40 bcm, including 17 bcm from the United States. European gas storage remains roughly 15% below seasonal averages, with inventories expected to enter winter at 74% capacity and decline to approximately 25% by spring. UBS consequently raised its fourth-quarter Dutch TTF gas price forecast to €75 per megawatt-hour from €62 previously. Its 2027 forecast increased to €45 from €40, reflecting expectations of a slower recovery in Qatari LNG exports and continued European efforts to phase out Russian gas. Under a prolonged disruption scenario accompanied by colder weather, UBS sees fourth-quarter TTF prices averaging €90/MWh, with potential peaks near €120/MWh. A faster recovery in Qatari shipments and milder temperatures could instead bring fourth-quarter prices towards €50/MWh.

items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd has suspended new bookings to Manila, Batangas and Subic Bay until the end of December, as worsening congestion and a chronic shortage of empty-container storage capacity disrupt Philippine supply chains. The German carrier stopped accepting bookings to the three gateways from all origins and across every trade lane on September 29, citing severe constraints on container returns. Existing bookings may also face cancellation or revised arrangements. The crisis centres on the Philippines’ longstanding trade imbalance, with significantly more laden containers arriving than departing, leaving carriers struggling to find space for empty boxes. Philippine Ports Authority general manager Jay Santiago has urged foreign shipping lines to establish additional empty-container depots, describing this as the quickest solution to the worsening logistics bottleneck. Mary Zapata, president of the Confederation of Truckers Associations of the Philippines, told local newspaper Daily Tribune that some operators have waited as long as 40 days to return empty boxes. The problems triggered industrial action earlier this month, prompting the Philippine Bureau of Customs to acknowledge the severe pressure on truckers, customs brokers, importers and exporters. Subic Bay waiting times, however, remain below 12 hours, while Batangas operations are described as normal.

items.summary: There have been two more pollution incidents arising from a similar arrangement. In both cases, an Oil Discharge Monitoring Equipment (ODME) overboard discharge pipe was routed through a bunker fuel tank before terminating at the ship’s side. Why These Arrangements Warrant Attention An overboard pipe routed through a bunker or cargo oil tank can create a single-point failure with potentially significant pollution consequences. If a defect develops in a section of pipe located between the isolation overboard valve and the vessel’s shell, fuel oil may enter the pipe downstream of the closed valve and continue flowing directly overboard. Recommended Actions The West of England strongly recommends that Members and ship managers review the overboard piping arrangements across their fleets, giving particular attention to any overboard pipe that passes through a bunker or cargo oil tank and is capable of creating a direct route between a tank containing oil and the sea following loss of pipe integrity. Members may wish to consider the following: Identify Vulnerable Arrangements Review piping diagrams, tank plans, construction drawings and onboard arrangements to identify any overboard pipe routed through a bunker or cargo oil tank. Review Maintenance and Inspection Programmes Planned maintenance systems should identify and specifically address concealed or difficult-to-access overboard pipework routed through oil tanks.

items.title: Stolt Nielsen: Waiting for chemicals to catch up
items.original_title: Stolt Nielsen: Waiting for chemicals to catch up
items.summary: Stolt-Nielsen’s 3Q26 core figures were in line with consensus but somewhat below our estimates, as higher bunker costs absorbed stronger spot rates. While the Middle East conflict has sent crude and product tanker earnings soaring, chemical tankers have captured only part of the momentum. Still, 4Q26 is expected to be modestly softer, but depleted chemical inventories point to a restocking cycle ahead. Stolt Tankers’ operating profit of USD 52.1m missed our USD 63m, as 40.5% higher spot rates were offset by bunker costs of USD 718/t (USD 500/t) and 22.1% lower spot volumes. Meanwhile, strong product tanker markets should keep swing tonnage out of chemical trades well into 2027. The diversified business model continues to support the investment case: non-tanker segments contributed to ~50% of 3Q26 EBITDA. Overall financial performance is expected to be somewhat softer compared to 3Q26. Thus, despite slightly reducing our near-term estimates, we raise our TP to NOK 405/sh. (385), mainly driven by the improved debt profile, following the Avenir LNG deconsolidation.

items.title: Port of Los Angeles Sets All-Time Monthly Cargo Record
items.original_title: Port of Los Angeles Sets All-Time Monthly Cargo Record
items.summary: The Port of Los Angeles handled 1,042,652 Twenty-Foot Equivalent Units (TEUs) in September, the busiest month in its 118-year history and more than 20,000 units more than the previous monthly record set in July 2025. The record month also capped the busiest quarter in Port history, with nearly 3 million TEUs moving across its docks from July through September. From June through September, the Port handled nearly 4 million TEUs, the strongest four-month stretch on record. “After its best month in history, the Port of Los Angeles remains an incredible economic engine both locally and nationally, creating good-paying, union jobs for Angelenos and maintaining Los Angeles’ status as a global competitor for trade and commerce,” said Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass. Los Angeles is strong because our Port is strong, and none of this would be possible without our talented, dedicated, and skilled workforce.” “September was a month for the record books, and it was part of an extraordinary run for the Port of Los Angeles,” said Seroka. “Consumer demand remains resilient, importers are replenishing inventories and more cargo is being allocated to Los Angeles as shippers navigate continued challenges along other global trade routes. Empty containers totaled approximately 371,206 TEUs, the highest monthly total in Port history.

items.title: Pakistan seeks alternative LNG supplies, braces for winter shortages amid Qatar force majeure
items.original_title: Pakistan seeks alternative LNG supplies, braces for winter shortages amid Qatar force majeure
items.summary: Pakistan is seeking alternative liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments and preparing to curtail supplies to some sectors after Qatar extended force majeure notices on deliveries to Islamabad until Nov. 5, Pakistani officials said on Wednesday, amid concerns about possible winter gas shortages in the South Asian nation. QatarEnergy halted production and declared force majeure in March, following attacks on its facilities during the United States-Iran conflict in the Middle East. “The government has given a threshold of $27 per MMBtu for purchase of spot LNG cargoes,” a Petroleum Division official told Arab News, referring to cargoes purchased from the international market for near-term delivery rather than under a long-term supply contract. “We will try our best to get maximum cargos from Qatar under the long-term agreement and since we have been able to import two cargos a month after the war broke out, we hope around 8-10 cargos can be imported if the current situation prevails,” the Petroleum Division official told Arab News, adding that Islamabad would need to use its diplomatic influence with Iran, the US and Qatar to facilitate the passage of the LNG shipments through the strait. Imported LNG accounted for about one-fifth of gas consumption in July 2025–March 2026, according to Pakistan’s latest economic survey.

items.title: Danaos plots Norwegian listing for bulker business
items.original_title: Danaos plots Norwegian listing for bulker business
items.summary: Greek owner Danaos is exploring a carve-out of its dry bulk business and the sale of a minority stake through a potential listing in Norway. The New York-listed John Coustas-led company said it has mandated investment banks to advise on a possible equity placement and listing, describing the move as part of a wider push to create value and boost shareholder returns. Danaos cautioned that there is no certainty a transaction will proceed and gave no timetable. The business sits under Danaos Bulk Inc and currently comprises 11 capesize bulkers on the water and four 211,000 dwt newcastlemaxes under construction for delivery in 2028. Splash tracked the expansion earlier this year when the owner moved into bulker newbuildings for the first time and subsequently doubled the programme to four ships. The latest addition to the operating fleet was the 2009-built, 182,425 dwt John Junior , formerly Hebei No.1 , which joined Danaos in March. A successful carve-out would leave Danaos with two more clearly defined shipping platforms, separating a bulker business that has grown to almost 2.8m dwt on a fully delivered basis from its much larger containership operation. As of the beginning of October, Danaos owned 78 boxships and had another 28 containerships under construction.

items.title: Shipping’s extraordinary boom refuses to peak
items.original_title: Shipping’s extraordinary boom refuses to peak
items.summary: Global shipping earnings have reached another extraordinary milestone, with Clarksons Research’s cross-sector ClarkSea Index surging 12% in a week to an unprecedented $84,951 a day, its fifth consecutive all-time high. The index, a widely followed overall earnings barometer, measures average daily earnings across tankers, bulk carriers, containerships and gas carriers, weighted by vessel numbers in each sector. It covers approximately 80% of global shipping capacity, providing a broad measure of the industry’s fortunes. The latest reading dwarfs the previous shipping supercycle’s 2007 peak of $50,714 a day. Average VLCC earnings jumped another 21% last week to $804,601 a day, while suezmaxes climbed 17% to $724,398 and aframaxes surged 46% to $393,951. Elsewhere, dry bulk has softened, with capesize earnings retreating 16% to $31,130 and overall bulker earnings slipping 3% to $22,319. VLGCs are enjoying record earnings, reaching $209,000 a day on the US Gulf-Japan route, although LNG carriers remain the conspicuous laggard, with modern spot earnings down 19% to $34,250. The present boom is universal, transcending shipping sectors, as demand remains robust and ton-miles have been added as ships detour around war zones by taking longer routes home.

items.title: Star Bulk sells down kamsarmax pair to Hermes
items.original_title: Star Bulk sells down kamsarmax pair to Hermes
items.summary: Nasdaq-listed Greek dry bulk heavyweight Star Bulk Carriers has agreed to sell a 35% ownership interest in two recently built kamsarmax bulkers to Itochu’s investment and asset-holding vehicle, Hermes World Maritime, while retaining commercial and technical management of both ships. The Petros Pappas-led owner identified the vessels as the 2026-built Star Ellie and Star Bella. Financial terms and the expected completion date have not been disclosed. The pair form part of Star Bulk’s three-vessel kamsarmax acquisition programme at Hengli, confirmed in November last year. Market sources previously valued similar vessels at approximately $36m to $38m apiece, although Star Bulk did not disclose its acquisition costs. Hermes has recently been building its exposure to the dry bulk market. The two-vessel package was valued at approximately $33.6m, with Hermes paying around $16.4m for its minority stake. The latest agreement extends Hermes’ investment beyond handysize tonnage into modern kamsarmaxes, while allowing Star Bulk to release part of its ownership exposure without giving up the ships’ management. Star Bulk puts its fleet at 138 bulkers totalling approximately 13.8m dwt on a fully delivered basis, including its remaining newbuilding commitments.

items.title: Ningbo Ocean eyes two car carriers in $480m leasing plan
items.original_title: Ningbo Ocean eyes two car carriers in $480m leasing plan
items.summary: China’s Ningbo Ocean Shipping is looking to add two 7,000 ceu LNG dual-fuel car carriers under a long-term leasing programme, with potential rental payments of up to $480m. The Shanghai-listed carrier disclosed the plan in a stock exchange filing, saying it or one of its subsidiaries intends to lease the vessels from a financial leasing company for a period of up to 20 years. Ningbo Ocean has yet to select a leasing partner or agree on the final financing terms. The company has also not identified the vessels, their source or delivery dates. The proposal remains subject to shareholder approval, with a vote scheduled for October 26. The move comes just two months after Ningbo Ocean entered the car carrier market with the 7,000 ceu Clean Star, which it chartered for two years at a reported $80,000 per day. The LNG dual-fuel vessel, built at CIMC Raffles in China and backed by Greek owner Atlas Maritime and Danish investment firm European Maritime Finance, began carrying Chinese-made vehicles to Europe in August, with calls including Gioia Tauro and Barcelona. Ningbo Ocean, controlled by Ningbo-Zhoushan Port Group, has traditionally concentrated on container and dry bulk shipping, building up its fleet through successive newbuilding programmes at Chinese yards.

items.title: Chinese shipping investor makes play for asphalt tanker owner Xin Yuan
items.original_title: Chinese shipping investor makes play for asphalt tanker owner Xin Yuan
items.summary: Chinese shipping entrepreneur Liu Jichun is seeking control of Hong Kong-listed asphalt tanker operator Xin Yuan Enterprises through a proposed cash takeover worth up to HK$771m ($99m). Liu’s investment vehicle Ocean Vivo has announced a voluntary conditional offer of HK$2.21 per share for the stock it does not already own, valuing Xin Yuan’s entire equity at approximately HK$972.4m ($125m). Ocean Vivo and parties acting in concert currently control 20.71% of the company, having built their position through off-market share purchases in March and July. The proposed combination would bring Xin Yuan’s asphalt tanker chartering business alongside Liu’s existing shipping interests, with the buyer indicating plans to explore cooperation and potential changes to the company’s asset structure. Xin Yuan operates 10 vessels with an aggregate capacity of approximately 92,000 dwt. The company also has two asphalt tanker newbuildings scheduled to join its fleet in the fourth quarter of 2026. The takeover remains conditional on Xin Yuan resuming share trading, which has been suspended since February 2025 following allegations concerning the company and certain directors. The current deadline for satisfying that precondition is October 30, although the buyer can extend it. Singapore-based Pioneer Logistics Holdings is looking to exit its indirect investment in Xin Yuan as part of the proposed transaction.
